description.narrative: Stöd till organisationen European Roma Rights Centre (ERRC) som arbetar för romers rättigheter. ERRC driver strategiska rättsfall, utövar påverkansarbete, utbildning och forskning för romers rättigheter i östra och sydöstra Europa.

Support to the organisation European Roma Rights Centre (ERRC) that works for Roma rights. The ERRC promotes Roma rights in Eastern and South-eastern Europe through strategic litigation, advocacy work, education, and research.

Ternipe childhood. Authorities responsible for child protection stop discriminate against Romani children and families, so that Romani children are no longer overrepresented among children in care.
Kherovnipe environment. Public authorities ensure that all Roma have access to secure tenure in integrated communities and with equal access to public services, so that Roma are no longer disproportionately living in environmentally degraded conditions.
Sicljovipe education. Authorities adopt and implement desegregation plans as well as policies that combat other forms of discrimination against Roma at school.
Sastipe health. Public health authorities guarantee that Romani women have access to non-segregated and otherwise equal reproductive healthcare.
Lila identity. Authorities ensure that every Romani person has a nationality and can prove it.
Piripnasko migration. Border guards and other officials end discrimination against Roma who travel to and move within the European Union.
Shngale police. Prosecutors and interior ministries acknowledge antigypsyism in policing and take the necessary steps to end it, particularly by punishing police who mistreat Roma.
The objectives are slightly rephrased from ERRC's strategy, in which they are labelled as theories of change related to ERRC's prioritised thematic areas.

In the past period, ERRC continued its operations around legal cases and mass complaints as the basis for advocacy and to hold authorities to account for discrimination. Advancements have been made related to the overall thematic objectives in different countries to varying extents. Through the strategic litigation, ERRC has continued to seek legal ground as a strategy for holding authorities accountable for upholding the human rights of Romani people. Complaints towards Equality Bodies and Ombudsperson institutions, ie not legal cases, were also ways to demand accountability. With court decisions and recommendations from equality bodies, ERRC has continued to push authorities to implement human rights and to end discrimination against Romani people. The court rulings and the recommendations provide accountability mechanisms for responsible institutions, and are important steps in changing policy and practice, including behaviour, within domestic authorities. This work usually takes several years and achieving a court decision or statement from an institution is a step on the way for authorities to change. ERRC also reports on some cases where institutions have changed.
At the end of 2024, the caseload in ODA countries were allocated as follows:
Albania 5

Kosovo 3
Moldova 13
Montenegro 1

TOTAL 112
Out of these 112 cases (58 % of ERRCs total caseload), 73 were pending before domestic bodies, 29 before the ECtHR, and 10 before UN treaty bodies.
Divided according to the thematic objectives, the caseload at the end of the 2024 showed:
Police 56

Grassroots legal mobilization efforts remained active across the Western Balkan six. ERRC continued to support local grassroot organizationsand activists to mobilize a critical mass of Romani people to seek justice for key issues for their communities, using accessible complaint mechanisms for which they do not require a lawyer. This has led to ERRC forging solid relationships with institutions such as Equality Bodies and Ombudsmans offices. Through them ERRC has been able to build precedent-setting cases from the ground up to allow for wider legal actions on similar issues which Roma face across the region.
The aim of the grassroots legal mobilization is to flood decision-making bodies with legal complaints, making the issues impossible to ignore. The approach has revealed patterns of discrimination, exposed overarching inequality, and lace legal advocacy into the hands of Romani communities themselves so they are better able to fight for the issues that really matter to them.
A total of 57 new mass complaints were submitted across the region. Of these, 14 have been concluded and 43 remain active. In total, 13 193 Roma individuals were assisted through the mass complaints.
North Macedonia: 14 cases, 5834 individuals assisted
Serbia 21 cases until July 2024; later integrated into the RISE project, 387 individuals assisted. Additionally, 2 more cases were submitted under the RISE project in September.
Kosovo 11 cases, 2557 individuals assisted.
Montenegro, 2 cases 2030 individuals assisted: both cases involved housing and environment issues.
Bosnia & Herzegovina, 9 cases, 2 385 individuals assisted.
Albania: No new mass complaints were submitted in 2024 due to integration into the RISE project framework.
In total, there are a total of 230 mass complaints submitted through ERRCs initiative since 2020 (141 active, 89 concluded), reflecting the long-term impact of ERRCs community empowerment strategy.
Gender and intersectionality
Efforts to ensure that Romani women appear as litigants continued during 2024. Women were the sole of predominant litigants in 10% of the cases in 2024, most of them representing particular forms of harm that Romani women face. ERRC recognized the need to continue these efforts and to do better at making sure that Romani women appear as litigants in the cases.
ERRC human rights monitors have received training on intersectionality to better support underrepresented groups.
Throughout 2024, ERRC has placed growing emphasis on addressing intersectional forms of discrimination in both individual complaints and in broader community-level mobilization efforts, as was set out in the workplan for 2024. This has highlighted the overlapping impacts of ethnicity, gender, age, and disability. The growing portfolio of intersectionality-focused litigation has laid the groundwork for stronger accountability mechanisms and more inclusive anti-discrimination frameworks.
Results from ERRCs advocacy, communication and research
ERRC continued its advocacy and awareness raising. In 2024 ERRC published 25 press releases and over 40 news posts related to relevant, unfolding news stories and our ongoing work.
ERRC research has contributed to awareness-raising, policy developments, and strategic litigation. Our monitors and researchers collect reliable, necessary data on the human rights situation of Roma across Europe to support ERRC advocacy work and litigation.
In 2024 ERRC published 8 research reports covering a variety of thematic areas, such as racist policing in the Western Balkans, the ongoing fight against online hate, inequal access to sport for Roma, Sinti, and Travellers, and the inequalities faced by Romani refugees from Ukraine.
ERRC also submitted written comments to 8 relevant international bodies, among them the UN Committee against Torture re. North Macedonia and Turkey, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination re. Albania and Greece, and the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child re. Albania. ERRCs submissions ensured that awareness of the reality of the situation for Romani communities was raised, and that inaction on the part of states was reported on and that they were held accountable.
ERRC also followed up on the implementation of European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) judgments in ERRC cases to ensure real change for Romani communities. ERRC submitted five Rule 9 communications to the Department of Execution of Judgments (DEJ), providing important updates and spotlighting ongoing efforts to tackle critical issues faced by Romani communities across Europe. These submissions covered three Roma-related cases from ODA countries, including a group of cases under Kitanovski and Others v. North Macedonia. This group included two Roma cases brought by the ERRC - X and Others and Memedov - which highlighted police abuse and failures in protecting Romani minors. Other cases addressed segregation and discrimination education, such as Elmazova and Others v. North Macedonia and X and Others v. Albania. These Rule 9 submissions were jointly submitted with the Macedonian Equality Body to push states to properly implement the Courts rulings and take concrete steps to end discrimination and exclusion.
